title: What can a glowing fibre tell us about a medieval document?
content:
Medieval charters are more than written records. They are physical objects, carefully produced and preserved, with materials that can tell us much about the people and practices behind them. In CHARM, we also have charters that have seals attached to them with parchment strips or cords. The attachment, with the seal, helped to authenticate documents and give them authority.

But what were these threads made of? Were they linen, silk, or another fibre? And how were their colours produced?

As part of the CHARM project, we are investigating the fibres used to attach seals to medieval Finnish charters, to see if they can provide a useful additional proxy in our project.

title: Did Mendel Breed Mice?
content:
We are delighted to share a new essay from our group, published open access in . Many genetics students have heard that Mendel first studied inheritance in mice, saw the segregation of fur colour, and switched to peas only when a disapproving bishop objected to a friar watching rodents mate. It is a wonderful story, but is it true?

The paper traces the tale back to its only source, Hugo Iltis, who interviewed people who had known Mendel and reported that he kept white and grey mice in his rooms at the abbey. Iltis himself presented any crossing experiments as his own speculation. The essay sets this against the real tensions of the time, including the hostility of Bishop Schaffgotsch towards St Thomas’s Abbey, and shows that the famous remark attributed to Mendel, that the bishop did not realise plants also have sex, is a modern literary invention with no historical basis.

That Mendel kept mice is plausible, but what he did with them remains unknown. The story, the paper argues, is a fine example of how anecdotes gather around famous scientists and of the temptation to read the past through what we already know.

title: A New Family Tree for the Nightshades
content:
We are proud to share a major new paper on the nightshade family, published open access in , the journal of the International Association for Plant Taxonomy. The study was led by Rocío Deanna, Marie Skłodowska-Curie fellow in our group, together with Richard Olmstead and an international team of Solanaceae experts.

Solanaceae comprise about 3000 species in 103 genera, among them some of the world’s most important crops. Decades of phylogenetic research have produced a confusing mix of names applied to groups at different ranks, many of them informal. To bring order to this, the team built a phylogeny of 1474 species, roughly half the family, from ten plastid and nuclear markers, and complemented it with genomic data from 97 of the 103 genera using the Angiosperms353 probe set.

title: The Living Genebanks of Mendel’s Moravia
content:
We are pleased to share a new historical paper from our group, published open access in . Genebanks are usually traced back to Nikolai Vavilov and his great seed collections of the 1920s. Yet a century earlier, in the region around Brno, a remarkable network of experimental gardens was already doing something very similar.

Known as herbaria viva, or living herbaria, these collections were established on aristocratic estates such as Lednice, in monastery gardens and in society nurseries. At Lednice, Theobald von Walberg arranged hundreds of native and foreign trees, crops and ornamentals side by side, kept seed samples as reference material and compared the yield and quality of introduced cultivars with local ones. In Brno, Jan Sedláček, Josef Zeman, Abbot Cyrill Napp and František Diebl promoted artificial pollination and hybridisation to breed new fruit and vine varieties suited to Moravian conditions.

title: A Mitogenome for the Downy Mildew That Threatens Roses and Berries
content:
We are very happy to congratulate Zoárd Kenessey on publishing the first paper of his PhD thesis in , the open access journal of the American Phytopathological Society, together with Hanna Susi.

Peronospora sparsa attacks economically important members of the rose family, including roses, Rubus hybrids, cloudberry and arctic bramble, a much loved Nordic berry. Despite its importance, genomic resources for the pathogen have remained very limited, and standard markers such as ITS often struggle to separate closely related downy mildews or detect cryptic species.

Zoárd assembled two complete mitochondrial genomes, one from arctic bramble collected at Kevo in Finnish Lapland in 2021, and one from a cloudberry specimen gathered near Petrozavodsk in 1899 and sequenced in the museums historical DNA laboratory. Remarkably, the two genomes differ by only 41 single nucleotide changes and three small indels, showing extremely low mitochondrial divergence across more than a century. These resources lay the foundation for better diagnostics, reliable discrimination among species of the Sparsa clade, and molecular surveillance of this pathogen.

title: Malta’s Endangered Sea Lavenders Reveal Chloroplast Genes That Disagree
content:
We are delighted to congratulate Dorita (Dolores R. Agius), our PhD student from Malta, on her new paper in . Limonium is a genus of more than 600 species centred in the Mediterranean, where hybridisation, apomixis and polyploidy make it one of the most taxonomically challenging groups of plants. Yet until now, no complete plastome had been sequenced from its Mediterranean heartland.

Dorita used PacBio HiFi reads to assemble the plastomes of Limonium melitense and L. zeraphae, two Maltese endemics listed as vulnerable. These salt tolerant shrubs cling to rocky shores just metres from the sea, a narrow habitat under heavy pressure from coastal activity on a small and densely populated island.

title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots en Route
content:
Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

Roots en Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.
